title: Warn before a useful capacity limit
trigger: Customers discover a usage limit only when an important job is interrupted.
action: Show actual consumption and remaining capacity early enough to plan, using a relevant threshold based on the product's workload. Explain the existing higher-capacity option and retain the current plan's normal functionality.
mechanism: Forewarning can turn an unexpected block into a considered upgrade decision.
guardrail: Use authoritative usage and reset rules; do not exaggerate exhaustion or invent a countdown.
measure: Appropriate capacity upgrades; surprise-limit contacts and unnecessary purchases.

title: Preserve blocked work through an upgrade
trigger: A user reaches a paid boundary after entering substantial information and loses that work during checkout.
action: Save the permitted draft and the attempted action, then resume it after verified entitlement is available. Explain what remains saved if the buyer cancels payment or stays on the current plan.
mechanism: Protecting invested effort can make evaluating an upgrade less disruptive.
guardrail: Never hold previously available work hostage; validate permissions and avoid replaying destructive actions automatically.
measure: Upgrades followed by successful task completion; lost-work reports.

title: Explain the paid capability at its use point
trigger: Clicking an unavailable feature opens a generic price table without explaining the benefit of this particular upgrade.
action: Describe the attempted capability, the supported result, and the plan that enables it within the task context. Show a concise truthful example of that capability using permitted data, then let the user continue or return.
mechanism: A benefit tied to an immediate job can make the purchase more concrete.
guardrail: Do not simulate unavailable results as if already delivered or hide requirements needed after purchase.
measure: Feature-motivated upgrades; refunds from expectation mismatch.

title: Compare upgrades with actual account entitlements
trigger: An existing account has add-ons, legacy grants, or custom access that makes the public plan comparison inaccurate for its upgrade.
action: Build the upgrade summary from the account's actual entitlements and the proposed resulting state. Identify genuinely new capabilities, retained grants, and any removed benefit instead of simply comparing two public plan names.
mechanism: A personally accurate comparison can reduce uncertainty about what an existing customer is really buying.
guardrail: Verify legacy, complimentary, and add-on treatment against the actual contract; do not imply already-owned features require another purchase.
measure: Correct suitable upgrades; lost-entitlement and duplicate-value complaints.

title: Recommend capacity from actual workload
trigger: Users cannot determine which higher tier will handle their existing workload.
action: Use verified recent usage and a clearly stated forecast assumption to suggest the smallest existing option that fits. Let the customer adjust unusual spikes or expected growth before choosing.
mechanism: A workload-based recommendation can make an abstract capacity ladder easier to evaluate.
guardrail: Label projections, account for reset periods and cost controls, and avoid automatically buying the recommended option.
measure: Upgrade fit and subsequent use; overbuying and repeat limit failures.

title: Let members request the exact upgrade
trigger: A non-billing team member encounters a useful paid feature but cannot authorize the purchase.
action: Provide an approval-request draft naming the attempted job, required capability, current account, and exact proposed offer. Let the member review it and use the organization's authorized route to the billing owner.
mechanism: A concrete internal request can bridge the gap between product need and buying authority.
guardrail: Do not send messages or expose private work without authorization; keep final purchase with an authorized buyer.
measure: Approved requests reaching paid use; unwanted messages and access mistakes.

title: Clarify billable membership before inviting
trigger: Adding a collaborator can trigger an unexpected paid-seat expansion.
action: Before an authorized invitation creates a billable seat, show the existing active-seat count, the recipient's intended role, and the applicable additional cost or limit. Offer a genuine non-billable role only when it fits the task.
mechanism: Predictable expansion reduces uncertainty about collaborating in the product.
guardrail: Do not change roles to avoid legitimate billing rules or send invitations without authorization.
measure: Successful collaborative expansion; seat-charge disputes.

title: Match temporary spikes to existing options
trigger: A short-lived workload spike makes the customer feel forced into a lasting tier increase.
action: If the product already offers suitable temporary capacity, show that option alongside the recurring upgrade with its exact scope and expiry. Explain which choice fits a one-off burst versus continuing need.
mechanism: A fitting alternative can reduce an all-or-nothing decision at a moment of demand.
guardrail: Do not invent a temporary product or promise automatic reversion; propose commercial changes separately if needed.
measure: Paid capacity purchases; unwanted ongoing charges and margin.

title: Suggest automation after repeated manual work
trigger: A customer repeatedly performs a manual task that an existing paid automation can actually handle.
action: At a relevant completion point, show the verified automation path and the specific repeated steps it would replace. Let the customer inspect and configure it before deciding whether the upgrade is worthwhile.
mechanism: A visible contrast with experienced effort can make an advanced capability's value tangible.
guardrail: Use real behavior and supported automation; avoid speculative time-saving claims or premature interruptions.
measure: Automation upgrades used successfully; failed setups and unused purchases.

title: Check integration readiness before upgrading
trigger: A paid integration is promoted even when the customer's external account or permissions cannot support it.
action: Run the supported non-destructive compatibility checks before purchase and explain remaining prerequisites. Offer the upgrade only with a clear route to completing the required connection.
mechanism: Reducing uncertainty about feasibility can make a qualified upgrade easier to justify.
guardrail: Do not request broader access than needed or treat a successful precheck as a guaranteed full integration.
measure: Integration upgrades reaching successful use; incompatibility refunds.

title: Recognize capabilities the customer already owns
trigger: A stale feature gate asks customers to buy something included in their current plan.
action: Reconcile entitlements and account context before showing an upgrade. Route already-entitled users to activation, permissions, or support recovery instead of another checkout.
mechanism: Correct recognition protects confidence and removes a false purchase barrier.
guardrail: Use authoritative access state and distinguish permission problems from genuinely missing commercial entitlement.
measure: Successful feature use; duplicate purchases and false-paywall complaints.

title: Respect a dismissed upgrade suggestion
trigger: The same promotion reappears on every visit after the customer has declined it.
action: Persist an appropriate dismissal or snooze and suppress the prompt until a meaningful change in need or the chosen reminder time. Keep upgrades discoverable through normal account controls.
mechanism: Respecting a deliberate choice may preserve attention and goodwill for a later relevant offer.
guardrail: Do not let suppression hide an actual service limit or charge notice; avoid inventing a reason to reset it.
measure: Later relevant upgrades; prompt fatigue and task interruption.

title: Save an upgrade for later evaluation
trigger: A buyer is interested in a capability but cannot decide during the current task.
action: Offer a saved evaluation item containing the feature, intended job, and current offer facts. Restore it in an appropriate account area, and draft a reminder only if the user requests an authorized communication.
mechanism: A preserved intention can make returning easier without forcing an immediate commitment.
guardrail: Revalidate prices and eligibility on return; saving an item must not start a trial or subscription.
measure: Saved evaluations becoming paid use; stale-offer confusion.

title: Keep a useful current-plan alternative
trigger: A paid feature blocks a task even though a legitimate simpler workflow exists on the current plan.
action: Explain the additional benefit of upgrading and offer the supported current-plan route alongside it. Preserve the user's work so the choice is about capability rather than recovering access.
mechanism: A reversible choice can make the upgrade feel deliberate and improve perceived fit.
guardrail: Do not cripple the existing route or claim the alternative is equivalent when meaningful limitations remain.
measure: Suitable upgrades and retained use; coerced-purchase refunds.

title: Guide the first use after upgrading
trigger: Payment succeeds but the newly purchased feature remains undiscovered or unconfigured.
action: Return the buyer to the relevant capability with its actual setup steps and a clear first successful action. Record whether the purchased addition is used rather than ending the journey at a payment confirmation.
mechanism: Connecting payment to immediate value can reinforce the reason for the upgrade.
guardrail: Wait for verified entitlement and keep configuration reversible where possible; do not fabricate success.
measure: Upgrades reaching first feature value; unused purchases and early churn.

title: Summarize achieved value at trial decision time
trigger: An existing trial ends with a generic payment demand that ignores what the user accomplished.
action: Show a concise account-specific summary of verified results, the capabilities used, and what each available continuation option retains. State the actual end behavior and charge before the buyer decides.
mechanism: Relevant remembered value can make the purchase decision more concrete.
guardrail: Do not exaggerate savings, imply data loss falsely, or count sample activity as customer achievement.
measure: Trial users reaching retained paid use; surprise charges and unused subscriptions.

title: Offer expansion after demonstrated success
trigger: Expansion prompts appear immediately after failed jobs or before the customer has used the original purchase.
action: Gate proactive expansion suggestions on an observed need and successful use of the current product. When an unresolved service issue exists, prioritize recovery and surface an upgrade only if it truly addresses the verified constraint.
mechanism: A relevant offer after achieved value may receive more considered attention than an untimely promotion.
guardrail: Do not suppress access to requested plan information or mislabel a product failure as a reason to pay more.
measure: Useful expansion; issue resolution, refunds, and account retention.

title: Explain paid value during complimentary access
trigger: A customer with temporary or complimentary access sees a purchase button for capabilities already available.
action: Show the current entitlement and its verified end condition, then explain what buying now changes, when billing starts, and any difference in access duration or features. Keep the existing free entitlement understandable.
mechanism: A clear incremental commitment can reduce accidental purchases and make a genuine continuation choice easier.
guardrail: Do not imply free access has expired or assume credits transfer; verify the exact commercial treatment.
measure: Deliberate paid continuations; duplicate-value refunds and confusion.

title: Support a deliberate future upgrade date
trigger: A customer wants a higher tier for a scheduled project but immediate activation does not match the need.
action: Where the billing system and offer support it, let the buyer choose or request a future effective date and preview the corresponding access and charge timing. Otherwise clearly present the currently supported immediate path.
mechanism: Aligning purchase timing with a concrete need can reduce unnecessary commitment friction.
guardrail: Treat new scheduling behavior as a commercial change; verify cancellation, availability, and execution semantics before release.
measure: Scheduled upgrades activated successfully; timing disputes and unused capacity.

title: Show the real quota reset alternative
trigger: A quota paywall omits when the current plan's allowance becomes available again.
action: Show the accurate reset date or rule beside the relevant upgrade option, and explain whether unfinished work remains saved. Let the customer choose between the added capacity and waiting for their existing entitlement.
mechanism: An understandable time-versus-capacity trade-off can support an informed purchase.
guardrail: Use the actual reset timezone and quota policy; do not invent urgency or imply unused credits roll over.
measure: Appropriate quota upgrades; waiting users retained and timing complaints.
